blocks.prompt: Read the story, then answer the questions. Take your time.
A Doctor for Your Teeth
blocks.text: A dentist is a doctor for your teeth. When you visit, you sit in a big chair that leans back. The dentist uses a small round mirror to see behind each tooth. A bright light helps them look. They count your teeth and check that your gums are pink and healthy. Little kids have twenty baby teeth. These baby teeth fall out one by one, and bigger grown-up teeth grow in to take their place. The dentist shows you how to brush and how to floss. Sugar can hurt your teeth, so it is good to brush after sweet food.

blocks.prompt: The Hardest Stuff in Your Body
blocks.text: Going to the dentist is how you keep your teeth working for a lifetime. Your teeth are covered in enamel, which is the hardest stuff in your whole body. Enamel is even harder than bone. But there is a catch. When enamel gets a hole in it, your body cannot grow it back the way a scrape on your knee heals. That hole is called a cavity, and the dentist has to fix it. Cavities start when tiny germs in your mouth feed on the sugar left over from your food. As they eat, the germs make acid, and the acid slowly wears through the enamel. A dentist uses a small mirror and a bright light to hunt for the first signs before a cavity grows large. Sometimes they take an x-ray, which is a special photo that shows the inside of a tooth. Brushing twice a day and cutting down on sugary drinks keeps most cavities away.

blocks.prompt: From the Barber's Chair to the Dentist's
blocks.text: People have worried about their teeth for a very long time. Archaeologists have found human teeth almost nine thousand years old with tiny, careful holes drilled into them, which means someone was already trying to treat toothaches back in the Stone Age. For most of history, though, there were no dentists. If a tooth hurt badly enough, a barber, of all people, would simply pull it out. Barbers cut hair and pulled teeth in the same shop. Modern dentistry really began with a French doctor named Pierre Fauchard in the early seventeen hundreds. He was the first person to write everything down in one place: how teeth are shaped, what causes decay, and how to repair a damaged tooth instead of yanking it. People now call him the father of modern dentistry. Today a checkup is calm and quick. The dentist seats you in a reclining chair and uses a small angled mirror to inspect surfaces your eyes could never reach. A thin metal pick, called an explorer, tests each tooth for soft spots. Clear x-ray images reveal trouble hidden between teeth or under the gum. Most of the visit is not about fixing problems at all. It is about catching them early, while they are still small enough to stop.

blocks.prompt: The War Being Fought in Your Mouth
blocks.text: Your mouth is one of the busiest places in your body, and it is never truly clean. Within minutes of brushing, a thin, invisible film called plaque begins forming on your teeth again. Plaque is not food. It is a living colony of bacteria, millions of them, held together in a sticky layer they build for themselves. These bacteria are not evil, and most do you no harm. The trouble starts with what they eat. Every time you swallow something sweet or starchy, the bacteria in the plaque get a meal too. As they digest those sugars, they release acid as a waste product. That acid sits against the tooth and begins dissolving the minerals out of the enamel, the glassy armor on the outside of every tooth. A single sugary snack can keep the acid working for around half an hour. Brush the plaque away, and the attack stops. Leave it, and day after day the acid drills deeper until it breaks through into the softer layer beneath. That is a cavity, and once enamel is gone, it does not grow back. This is why the dentist's advice sounds so simple and yet matters so much. Brushing and flossing physically scrape the bacteria off before they can do damage. Fluoride, the mineral added to most toothpaste and to a lot of tap water, actually rebuilds weakened enamel and makes it more resistant to acid. Cutting down on how often, not just how much, you eat sugar gives your teeth long stretches of peace to recover. A dentist does more than fix broken teeth. A good one is teaching you how to make sure fewer of them ever break in the first place.

blocks.prompt: Three Centuries from Pliers to Prevention
blocks.text: For most of human history, a toothache was something you simply endured, and dentistry, when it existed at all, was mostly a matter of removal. If a tooth rotted and the pain grew unbearable, someone stronger than you pulled it out, often with pliers and no way to numb the shock. In medieval Europe that someone was frequently the local barber, whose shop offered haircuts, shaves, and extractions from the same chair. The striped red and white pole still seen outside some barbershops is a leftover from those days, when the trade mixed grooming with minor surgery. Care meant reacting to disaster after it had already struck. The shift from pulling teeth to saving them is surprisingly recent. In 1728 a French surgeon named Pierre Fauchard published a thick book that gathered, for the first time, everything then known about the mouth. He described the anatomy of teeth, argued that decay was a disease with causes rather than a punishment, and detailed ways to repair a damaged tooth instead of discarding it. Historians credit that book with founding modern dentistry, and it reframed the whole job. The dentist was no longer a puller of teeth but a keeper of them. Understanding why teeth decay only came later, and it is stranger than most people expect. A cavity is not really damage done to you by candy. It is damage done by living organisms that candy happens to feed. The surface of every tooth is coated within hours by plaque, a sticky biofilm built by colonies of bacteria. When you eat sugar, those bacteria eat it too, and their waste product is acid. The acid dissolves minerals out of the enamel, the hard outer shell of the tooth, and if the assault is repeated often enough the enamel finally fails. Because enamel is not living tissue, it cannot repair itself the way skin or bone does. Once the hole opens, only a dentist can close it. That single fact explains why the modern profession has quietly changed its goal again. The most important work now happens before anything breaks. Fluoride hardens enamel and helps rebuild the earliest weak spots. Regular cleanings strip away plaque the toothbrush misses. X-rays and a sharp eye catch decay while it is still microscopic. A good dentist measures success not by how many teeth are drilled and filled, but by how many never need to be. In three centuries the field has moved from the barber's pliers to the prevention of harm that has not happened yet, and that is a quiet kind of progress worth noticing.
